titre: Cajal and Golgi, One Nobel Prize for Two Opposing Theories
accroche: In 1906, the Nobel committee rewards two mutually exclusive theories in equal shares, and one of the laureates says so in his own speech.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 10, 1906, the Nobel committee awards Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal equal shares “in recognition of their work on the structure of the nervous system.” It is the first time a Nobel Prize in Medicine is shared, and the two laureates defend theories that exclude each other.

## One Method, Two Opposite Readings

In 1873, Golgi develops a silver nitrate stain, the “reazione nera,” which stains only a random fraction of nerve cells, but stains them whole, down to the finest branches. Under the microscope, Golgi sees a continuous network, a kind of fused tissue in which nerve extensions join without interruption: the reticular theory.

Cajal discovers the method in 1887 in Madrid, through Luis Simarro. He refines it, applies it to younger and better-prepared tissues, and reaches the opposite conclusion. What Golgi takes for a fused network, Cajal sees as distinct individual cells, which touch without merging: the neuron doctrine.

The two men use the same tool and look, quite literally, at preparations obtained by the same technique. They do not draw the same architecture of the nervous system from them.

## The Committee Rules by Half

The Nobel committee's archives, made public afterward, show that Golgi's persistent attachment to the reticular theory, when the neuron doctrine had already won the support of most neuroscientists of the day, was among the weak points of his case. The prize is awarded to him all the same, on equal terms with Cajal.

Golgi yields nothing. The day after the ceremony, in his own Nobel lecture, he chooses as his subject the neuron doctrine, in order to go on opposing it. He announces it himself, with a certain irony: “It may seem strange that, having always opposed the neuron theory, while acknowledging that its starting point lies in my own work, I chose this question of the neuron as the subject of my lecture, at a time when this doctrine is generally considered to be falling out of favor.”

## What Electron Microscopy Settled

The debate does not close that day. It takes until the 1950s and the arrival of electron microscopy to settle it for good: observations show a measurable space, about 10 to 20 nanometers, between the pre- and post-synaptic elements, the synaptic cleft. No cytoplasmic fusion between neurons. Golgi was right about the method; Cajal was right about what it showed.

carte.punch: Golgi and Cajal shared a Nobel Prize while each defending the opposite of the other.
carte.idee: Golgi sees in his own stains a fused nerve network; Cajal, with the same method, sees distinct cells. The 1906 Nobel committee rewards them in equal shares, and Golgi defends, in his own lecture, the thesis that electron microscopy would invalidate in the 1950s.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The lecture given by Cajal the day after Golgi's.

quiz.question: How was the debate between the reticular theory (Golgi) and the neuron doctrine (Cajal) finally settled?
choix: Golgi eventually publicly rallied to Cajal's position before his death
A vote of the Nobel committee validated the neuron doctrine in 1906
Electron microscopy in the 1950s revealed a measurable space between neurons, with no fusion
Cajal discovered a new staining method that replaced Golgi's
quiz.explication: The 1906 Nobel Prize settled no scientific debate: Golgi maintained his position even in his own Nobel lecture. It was electron microscopy, in the 1950s, that revealed the synaptic cleft, a space of about 10 to 20 nanometers between neurons, definitively confirming the neuron doctrine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the stain Golgi developed in 1873, called the reazione nera, make it possible to observe?
choix: It stains all nerve cells, but only their nucleus
It stains a random fraction of cells, but whole, down to the finest branches
It stains only glial cells, never neurons
It makes synapses visible without staining the rest of the cell
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Golgi's reazione nera stains only a random fraction of nerve cells, but stains them whole, down to their finest branches, which allowed the two opposite readings by Golgi and Cajal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the Nobel committee's archives reveal as a weak point of Golgi's case in 1906?
choix: His stubborn refusal to publish his results before the prize was awarded
His lack of recognized collaborators in his own laboratory
His persistent attachment to the reticular theory, overtaken by the neuron doctrine
An accusation of plagiarism brought against him by an Italian colleague
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The archives show that Golgi's attachment to the reticular theory, when the neuron doctrine had already won the support of most researchers, was among the weak points noted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Through whom does Cajal discover Golgi's method in 1887, in Madrid?
choix: Camillo Golgi in person, at a congress
An article published in a French journal
His own anatomy professor at the University of Zaragoza
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is through Luis Simarro that Cajal discovers Golgi's method in 1887 in Madrid, before refining it and arriving at a reading opposite to its inventor's.
